title: How does Structured Streaming integrate with Kafka (`readStream.format("kafka")` for source, `writeStream.format("kafka")` for sink), and what delivery semantics does it provide (exactly-once with checkpointing + idempotent sinks)?

s1_definition.profdef: Structured Streaming integrates with Kafka through a built-in source and sink. As a source you use `spark.readStream.format("kafka")` with options such as the bootstrap servers and the topic to subscribe to, and Spark reads the topic as an unbounded DataFrame with columns like key, value, topic, partition, offset, and timestamp. As a sink you use `df.writeStream.format("kafka")` with the bootstrap servers and a target topic, writing rows (whose value and optional key columns you prepare) back to Kafka. Spark tracks the Kafka offsets it has consumed in its checkpoint, so on the read side it provides at-least-once by default and effectively exactly-once source semantics via checkpointed offsets; on the write side exactly-once end-to-end requires the sink to be idempotent or transactional, which for Kafka means idempotent producers and deduplicated downstream consumption.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India Kafka is the central mail room where every transaction message is dropped and picked up. Structured Streaming's Kafka source is a clerk who reads mail from a named mailbox (topic), remembering in a logbook exactly which letters have been read so that after a break they resume at the right letter — never skipping, and never re-counting already-finished work. The Kafka sink is a clerk who posts processed results back into another mailbox. To guarantee each result is posted exactly once even after a hiccup, the posting clerk stamps each letter with a unique id (idempotent producer) so the mail room ignores accidental resends.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structured Streaming integrates with Kafka through a built-in source and sink. As a source you use `spark.readStream.format("kafka")` with options such as the bootstrap servers and the topic to subscribe to, and Spark reads the topic as an unbounded DataFrame with columns like key, value, topic, partition, offset, and timestamp. As a sink you use `df.writeStream.format("kafka")` with the bootstrap servers and a target topic, writing rows (whose value and optional key columns you prepare) back to Kafka. Spark tracks the Kafka offsets it has consumed in its checkpoint, so on the read side it provides at-least-once by default and effectively exactly-once source semantics via checkpointed offsets; on the write side exactly-once end-to-end requires the sink to be idempotent or transactional, which for Kafka means idempotent producers and deduplicated downstream consumption.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India Kafka is the central mail room where every transaction message is dropped and picked up. Structured Streaming's Kafka source is a clerk who reads mail from a named mailbox (topic), remembering in a logbook exactly which letters have been read so that after a break they resume at the right letter — never skipping, and never re-counting already-finished work. The Kafka sink is a clerk who posts processed results back into another mailbox. To guarantee each result is posted exactly once even after a hiccup, the posting clerk stamps each letter with a unique id (idempotent producer) so the mail room ignores accidental resends.

**One line to remember:** Use readStream.format("kafka") to consume a topic as an unbounded DataFrame and writeStream.format("kafka") to produce back; checkpointed offsets give exactly-once on the source side, and idempotent/transactional sinks give exactly-once end-to-end.

sections.s2_technical:
On the source side you configure `format("kafka")` with `kafka.bootstrap.servers` and a subscription — `subscribe` for a fixed topic list, `subscribePattern` for a regex, or `assign` for specific partitions. Spark exposes each Kafka record as a row with key and value as binary, plus topic, partition, offset, and timestamp. You typically cast the value to a string or parse it from JSON or Avro: `selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING)")` then a `from_json`. You can bound how much each micro-batch reads with `maxOffsetsPerTrigger`, which is the main back-pressure control for a Kafka source.

Offset management on read is automatic and lives in the checkpoint, not in Kafka's consumer group. Structured Streaming does not rely on Kafka to commit offsets; it records the start and end offsets of each batch in its own checkpoint offset log. This is what makes replay and exactly-once possible: on restart Spark resumes from its checkpointed offsets, so it neither skips nor reprocesses committed batches. You control where a brand-new query starts with `startingOffsets` set to earliest or latest.

On the sink side you prepare a DataFrame with a `value` column (and optionally `key`, `topic`, `partition`, `headers`) and call `writeStream.format("kafka")` with the bootstrap servers and a target topic. Spark serializes each row into a Kafka record. A checkpoint location is mandatory for the write query too, because that is where it tracks which input offsets have been fully produced to the output topic.

Delivery semantics depend on both sides. The Kafka source with checkpointed offsets gives effectively exactly-once consumption of the source. For the full pipeline to be exactly-once, the write must not create visible duplicates on retry. With the Kafka sink you enable idempotent producers so that a retried send after a transient failure is deduplicated by the broker, and downstream consumers should still be prepared to deduplicate by a business key because Kafka's producer idempotence is per producer session. Where a sink is not naturally idempotent, you use transactional writes or an upsert by key to achieve exactly-once.

A senior-level nuance is that end-to-end exactly-once is a property of the whole chain, not just Spark. Spark guarantees it will reprocess uncommitted batches on recovery; the sink must guarantee that reprocessing does not produce duplicate effects. For a Kafka-to-Kafka pipeline that means idempotent or transactional producers plus idempotent consumers keyed on a stable business id such as a transaction id. For a Kafka-to-database pipeline it means an upsert on the primary key inside a foreachBatch. Designing the sink for idempotency is the real work of exactly-once, and claiming exactly-once without it is a common and dangerous mistake in banking pipelines.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India publishes every transaction to a Kafka topic. A streaming job must consume that topic, parse the JSON, and keep resuming from exactly where it left off across restarts. This is the Kafka source with checkpointed offsets.

Problem 2 — The job enriches each transaction and must publish the result to an output topic without creating duplicates when a batch is retried after a transient failure. This is the Kafka sink with idempotent producers plus a stable business key.

Problem 3 — A downstream consumer must still protect itself against any residual duplicate by deduplicating on the transaction id, because exactly-once is an end-to-end property.

The demo simulates reading transaction messages with tracked offsets, producing enriched results stamped with the transaction id as the Kafka key, and a downstream consumer that deduplicates by that key, logging how a retried batch does not create a duplicate downstream.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Kafka topic with three transaction records T1, T2, T3 at offsets 0, 1, 2, each keyed by its transaction id.

Step 1: Batch A polls the source. The committed offset starts at minus one, so all three records are fresh. They are passed to the sink.

Step 2: The idempotent sink produces all three, recording T1, T2, T3 as delivered keys. Three new records are delivered.

Step 3: The source commits offset 2 to the checkpoint, meaning batches up to offset 2 are fully processed. On a real restart Spark would resume after offset 2.

Step 4: A transient failure is simulated where T3 is re-sent before its commit was durable. The sink sees T3's key already delivered, so it ignores the duplicate and delivers zero new records. This is the idempotent sink turning at-least-once reprocessing into exactly-once effect downstream.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Polled 3 records after offset -1
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Produced enriched record key=T1
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Produced enriched record key=T2
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Produced enriched record key=T3
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Batch A delivered 3 records
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Committed offset 2 to checkpoint
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    --- simulated retry of last record after transient failure ---
2026-10-30 05:18:00 WARNING Duplicate key T3 ignored (idempotent)
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Retry delivered 0 NEW records (T3 dedup → 0)
2026-10-30 05:18:00 INFO    Kafka streaming exactly-once demo complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Structured Streaming integrates with Kafka through a built-in source and sink. As a source you use readStream.format("kafka") with the bootstrap servers and a subscription, and Spark exposes the topic as an unbounded DataFrame whose rows carry key, value, topic, partition, offset, and timestamp; you typically cast or parse the value from JSON or Avro and control intake with maxOffsetsPerTrigger for back-pressure. As a sink you prepare a value and optional key column and call writeStream.format("kafka") with a target topic, and a checkpoint location is mandatory on both the read and write side.

The crucial point about offsets is that Structured Streaming tracks consumed offsets in its own checkpoint, not in Kafka's consumer group. That is what lets it resume exactly where it left off and makes replay deterministic, giving effectively exactly-once consumption of the source. But end-to-end exactly-once is a property of the whole chain: Spark guarantees it will reprocess a batch that was started but not committed, so the sink must guarantee that reprocessing does not create duplicate effects. For a Kafka sink that means idempotent or transactional producers, and downstream consumers should still deduplicate on a stable business key such as the transaction id, because producer idempotence is per session.

At the National Bank of India I built a Kafka-to-Kafka enrichment job exactly this way. The source consumed the transactions topic with offsets tracked in an S3 checkpoint, and the sink wrote to an enriched topic keyed by transaction id with idempotent producers, while downstream services deduplicated by that same id. When a batch was retried after a transient failure, the duplicate was ignored downstream, so the effect was exactly-once. In interviews I summarize it as: readStream and writeStream with format kafka, offsets in Spark's checkpoint for exactly-once source semantics, and idempotent or transactional sinks keyed on a business id for exactly-once end-to-end — and I stress that claiming exactly-once without an idempotent sink is a dangerous mistake.
